According to the course materials, specifically in the section on "Encoders", it is stated that "An encoder is a digital circuit that performs the inverse operation of a decoder. An encoder has 2" (or less) input lines and n output lines. The output lines generate the binary code corresponding to the input value."

This means that an encoder can have either 2^n input lines or fewer, and it will have n output lines. The output lines will produce the binary code that corresponds to the input value.

For example, the octal-to-binary encoder mentioned in the course materials has 8 input lines (one for each octal digit) and 3 output lines that generate the corresponding binary number.

To summarize:

* An encoder has 2^n (or less) input lines
* An encoder has n output lines
* The output lines generate the binary code corresponding to the input value

The statement "(It must be realized that this type of connection cannot be done with gates that do not have three-state outputs" is a crucial point in understanding the construction of a bus system with three-state buffers.

According to the course materials, specifically in the section on "Three-State Bus Buffers", it is stated that "The construction of a bus system with three-state buffers is demonstrated in Fig. 4-5. The outputs of four buffers are connected together to form a single bus line. (It must be realized that this type of connection cannot be done with gates that do not have three-state outputs .)"

This means that the ability to connect multiple gates together to form a common bus line without endangering loading effects is a unique feature of three-state gates. The high-impedance state of a three-state gate provides this special feature, allowing a large number of three-state gate outputs to be connected with wires to form a common bus line.

As mentioned in the course materials, "The high-impedance state behaves like an open circuit, which means that the output is disconnected and does not have a logic significance." This is what enables the connection of multiple three-state gates to a single bus line without causing any issues.

To illustrate this, let's consider the example given in the course materials, where the outputs of four buffers are connected together to form a single bus line. The control inputs to the buffers determine which of the four normal inputs will communicate with the bus line, and no more than one buffer may be in the active state at any given time.

The use of a decoder, as shown in the diagram, ensures that only one three-state buffer has access to the bus line while all other buffers are maintained in a high-impedance state. This is achieved by using the enable input of the decoder to control the state of the buffers.

In summary:

* The connection of multiple gates to form a common bus line requires three-state gates.
* The high-impedance state of a three-state gate allows it to be connected to a bus line without endangering loading effects.
* The use of a decoder ensures that only one three-state buffer has access to the bus line at any given time.
* This is a unique feature of three-state gates, and it is not possible to achieve this type of connection with gates that do not have three-state outputs.

As we discussed earlier, encoders and decoders are related concepts, and understanding how they work is essential in designing digital circuits. The use of three-state gates and decoders is a crucial aspect of constructing a bus system, and it is essential to understand how they work together to enable the connection of multiple gates to a single bus line.
